topic.title: Solving 2 × 2 simultaneous equations with matrices
topic.subject: further-maths
topic.examWeightHint: Unit 1 is one two-hour calculator paper of 100 marks, sat every Summer. The shape is 'find the inverse' then 'hence, using a matrix method, solve', for about 2 + 4 marks: Summer 2025 Q5, where the inverse was very well answered and part (ii) was not, because many solved by substitution or elimination despite the instruction and received no marks, and several who did use matrices struggled with the layout. The report also notes the type had not appeared recently, so it is due. Schemes give MW for the pair written as AX = B, M for the determinant, M for the inverse, M for the product and W for x and y named.

When the question names the matrix method, elimination earns nothing

sheet.howExamined: Unit 1 is one two-hour calculator paper of 100 marks, sat every Summer. The shape is 'find the inverse' then 'hence, using a matrix method, solve', for about 2 + 4 marks. Summer 2025 Q5 is the example in our evidence: the inverse was very well answered, and part (ii) was not, because many solved by substitution or elimination despite the instruction and received no marks; several who did use matrices struggled with the layout. The report also records that the type had not appeared recently, which makes it due. The scheme gives MW for the pair written as AX = B, M for the determinant, M for the inverse, M for the product and W for x and y named, with follow-through from the inverse in the earlier part.
traps: Solving by elimination or substitution when the question names the matrix method, which earns nothing at all (Summer 2025 FM1 Q5)
Laying the matrix method out so that the examiner cannot follow it (Summer 2025 FM1 Q5)
Copying coefficients before both equations are lined up as ax + by = c
Leaving a slot empty where an equation has no term in one unknown
Reading the coefficients down the columns instead of across the rows
Writing the constants into the coefficient matrix instead of a column of their own
Multiplying the inverse on the wrong side (Summer 2018 FM1 Q5)
Leaving the answer as a column instead of naming x and y (Summer 2025 FM1 Q5)
Giving the two values the wrong way round (Summer 2025 FM1 Q5)
Not recognising that a zero determinant means there is no unique solution (Summer 2023 FM1 Q6)

steps.working: Copy the numbers into three matrices: $\begin{pmatrix}4 & 3 \\ 2 & 5\end{pmatrix}$ for the coefficients, a column for $x$ and $y$, and $\begin{pmatrix}18 \\ 16\end{pmatrix}$ for the constants.
steps.decision: This line is transcription, not mathematics, and it earns a mark before any arithmetic. Both equations are already in the right form here, so nothing has to be rearranged.
The determinant on its own line. A zero here would mean the pair has no unique solution, so it is worth knowing before any more work is done.
The same three actions as any inverse. From this point the question is an ordinary matrix equation.

options: Because the pair is now AX = B, and an inverse is what undoes a multiplying matrix
Because the determinant has to be cancelled from both sides
Because the two equations can be added together
whyMenu.explain: Once the pair is written as a matrix equation, nothing about it is new: pre-multiply both sides by the inverse.

steps.decision: The inverse goes in front of the constants. The product of a two by two and a column is a column, which is what the two unknowns need.

steps.working: Reading the column off: $x = 3$ and $y = 2$. Checking in both equations: $4(3) + 3(2) = 18$ and $2(3) + 5(2) = 16$.
steps.decision: The column is not the answer line. Name both values, and substitute them into both original equations: that check costs twenty seconds and catches every slip above it.

twin.stem: Solve the simultaneous equations $2x + 3y = 14$ and $3x + 5y = 22$, using a matrix method. Give the values of $x$ and $y$.

items.stem:
Three quick checks on what this lesson is built from. None of them is the new method, so answer from what you already know.
Rearrange $5x = 11 - 2y$ so that both letters are on the left.

options.feedback: The term in $y$ crosses the equals sign and changes sign.
Moving $-2y$ across makes it $+2y$, not $-2y$.
The $11$ was already on the right and does not move, so its sign is unchanged.
The determinant is $1$, so swapping and negating is the whole of it.
The leading diagonal swapped and the other one kept its signs.
The signs changed and the leading diagonal never swapped.

items.stem: A $2 \times 2$ matrix is multiplied by a $2 \times 1$ column. What shape is the answer?

options.feedback: The inner numbers match and the outer two give the shape, so the answer is a column.
The columns of the answer come from the second matrix, which has one.
Rows come first: the answer has as many rows as the first matrix.

items.stem: For the pair $4x + 3y = 18$ and $2x + 5y = 16$, which is the coefficient matrix?

options.feedback: One equation to a row, in the order the terms are written.
The coefficients have been read down the columns instead of across the rows.
The constants have gone into the coefficient matrix. They belong in a column of their own.

items.stem: An equation in a pair reads $3y = 12$, with no term in $x$. What goes in its $x$ slot?

options.feedback: A missing term is a zero. The row has to be complete for the product to reproduce the equation.
A matrix has no empty slots: leaving one out would change its shape.
A coefficient of $1$ would put an $x$ into the equation that is not there.

items.stem: A pair has been written as $AX = B$. What comes next?
items.skill: The method once the pair is transcribed

options.feedback: From here it is an ordinary matrix equation, with the inverse in front.
The inverse goes in front of both sides. $BA^{-1}$ is a different product, and here it does not even exist.

options.text: Add the two equations to remove one unknown
options.feedback: That is elimination. When the question names the matrix method, elimination earns nothing.

items.stem: Solving a pair gives the column $\begin{pmatrix}3 \\ 2\end{pmatrix}$. What should be written on the answer line?

options.feedback: The top entry is $x$ and the bottom is $y$.
The two values have swapped. The column is read top to bottom in the order the unknowns were written.
The question asked for two values, so both have to be named. A column is not an answer line.

items.stem: The coefficient matrix of a pair has determinant $0$. What does that tell you?

options.text: There is no unique solution, because the matrix has no inverse
options.feedback: The two equations describe parallel lines, so they never meet at a single point.
The determinant says nothing about the values; it says the method cannot run.

options.text: The pair must be solved by elimination instead
options.feedback: Elimination would not find a unique solution either: there is not one to find.

emphasis: You must use a matrix method

context.setting: The whole route on a pair with a positive determinant

parts.stem:
Solve the simultaneous equations
$4x + 3y = 18$
$2x + 5y = 16$
You must use a matrix method.
Give the values of $x$ and $y$.

scheme.for: $\begin{pmatrix}4 & 3 \\ 2 & 5\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}0 \\ 0\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}18 \\ 16\end{pmatrix}$ with the unknowns in the middle column
$X = A^{-1}B$, with the inverse in front

hints: Copy the coefficients and the constants into matrices first.
Then it is a matrix equation: find the inverse and pre-multiply.
Read the two values off the column and name them.
parts.workedSolution:
Writing the pair as $AX = B$ gives $A = \begin{pmatrix}4 & 3 \\ 2 & 5\end{pmatrix}$ and $B = \begin{pmatrix}18 \\ 16\end{pmatrix}$.
$\det A = 14$, so $A^{-1} = \frac{1}{14}\begin{pmatrix}5 & -3 \\ -2 & 4\end{pmatrix}$.
$X = A^{-1}B = \begin{pmatrix}3 \\ 2\end{pmatrix}$, so $x = 3$ and $y = 2$.
Checking in both equations: $4(3) + 3(2) = 18$ and $2(3) + 5(2) = 16$.

commonErrors.feedback: The two values are right and they have swapped places. The top entry of the column is $x$ and the bottom is $y$, so $x = 3$.

$x - y = -1$

Both original equations check out with those values.

parts.stem:
The matrix $A = \begin{pmatrix}2 & 3 \\ 3 & 5\end{pmatrix}$.
Find $A^{-1}$.
Write the answer as a matrix.
hints: Determinant first, then swap and negate.

commonErrors.feedback: The leading diagonal swapped and $b$ and $c$ kept their signs. The other diagonal changes sign, giving $\begin{pmatrix}5 & -3 \\ -3 & 2\end{pmatrix}$.

parts.stem:
Hence solve the simultaneous equations
$2x + 3y = 14$
$3x + 5y = 22$
You must use a matrix method.
Give the values of $x$ and $y$.

scheme.for: the pair written as $AX = B$ with $B = \begin{pmatrix}14 \\ 22\end{pmatrix}$
$X = A^{-1}B$, using the inverse from part (a)
the product worked row by column

hints: The coefficients are already the matrix $A$ from part (a).
Put the constants in a column and pre-multiply.
parts.workedSolution:
The pair is $AX = B$ with $B = \begin{pmatrix}14 \\ 22\end{pmatrix}$.
Using the inverse from part (a), $X = A^{-1}B = \begin{pmatrix}5 & -3 \\ -3 & 2\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}14 \\ 22\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}4 \\ 2\end{pmatrix}$.
So $x = 4$ and $y = 2$, and both values satisfy both equations.

commonErrors.feedback: Both values are right and they are the wrong way round. The top of the column is $x$.

questions.solutionProgram: a: $\det A = (2)(5) - (3)(3) = 1$. Swapping and negating gives $A^{-1} = \begin{pmatrix}5 & -3 \\ -3 & 2\end{pmatrix}$. || b: The pair is $AX = B$ with $B = \begin{pmatrix}14 \\ 22\end{pmatrix}$. Using the inverse from part (a), $X = A^{-1}B = \begin{pmatrix}5 & -3 \\ -3 & 2\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}14 \\ 22\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}4 \\ 2\end{pmatrix}$. So $x = 4$ and $y = 2$, and both values satisfy both equations.

parts.stem:
A stationer sells notebooks at $n$ pounds each and pens at $p$ pounds each.
3 notebooks and 2 pens cost 19 pounds.
5 notebooks and 4 pens cost 33 pounds.
Write down two equations in $n$ and $p$.
hints: Each sentence about a total cost becomes one equation.
parts.workedSolution: 3 notebooks at $n$ pounds and 2 pens at $p$ pounds give 3n + 2p = 19 and 5n + 4p = 33.

parts.stem:
Solve your two equations to find the price of a notebook and the price of a pen.
You must use a matrix method.
Give the values of $n$ and $p$.

scheme.for: the pair written as $AX = B$ with $A = \begin{pmatrix}3 & 2 \\ 5 & 4\end{pmatrix}$

hints: Copy the coefficients from your two equations into a matrix.
Then it is a matrix equation.
parts.workedSolution:
$A = \begin{pmatrix}3 & 2 \\ 5 & 4\end{pmatrix}$ and $B = \begin{pmatrix}19 \\ 33\end{pmatrix}$.
$\det A = 2$, so $A^{-1} = \frac{1}{2}\begin{pmatrix}4 & -2 \\ -5 & 3\end{pmatrix}$.
$X = A^{-1}B = \begin{pmatrix}5 \\ 2\end{pmatrix}$, so a notebook costs 5 pounds and a pen costs 2 pounds.
Checking: 3(5) + 2(2) = 19 and 5(5) + 4(2) = 33.

findTheMistake.stem: Órla was asked to solve $4x + 3y = 18$ and $2x + 5y = 16$, using a matrix method. Her working:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong:
Every line of this is correct arithmetic, and both values at the end are right.
Line 3 is where the marks go: it starts an elimination. The question named the matrix method, so no part of this route earns anything, however accurate it is.
The line that belongs there writes the pair as $AX = B$, with the coefficients in a matrix and the constants in a column.
correction: write the pair as AX = B with A = (4 3 ; 2 5) and B = (18 ; 16)
X = A inverse x B = (3 ; 2), so x = 3 and y = 2
findTheMistake.feedback: This is the hardest kind of mistake to accept, because nothing in it is wrong: the arithmetic is clean and the answer is right. What the examiners mark here is the method the question named, and the report for that series records correct elimination solutions earning nothing at all. Read the instruction before the equations, every time.

prompts.prompt: How is a pair of simultaneous equations written as a matrix equation?
prompts.answer: The coefficients go into a $2 \times 2$ matrix, one equation to a row; the unknowns go into a column; the constants go into a column on the other side, giving $AX = B$.

prompts.prompt: What has to be done to the equations before the coefficients are copied?
prompts.answer: Line them up as $ax + by = c$, with both letters on the left in the same order and the number alone on the right.

prompts.prompt: One equation of a pair has no term in $x$. What goes in its slot?
prompts.answer: A zero. Every slot of the coefficient matrix has to be filled for the product to reproduce the equations.

prompts.prompt: Once the pair is $AX = B$, how is it solved?
prompts.answer: $X = A^{-1}B$: find the determinant, build the inverse, and pre-multiply the column of constants.

prompts.prompt: The product gives a column. Why is that not the answer?
prompts.answer: The question asked for two values, so both have to be named: the top entry is the first unknown and the bottom entry the second.

prompts.prompt: How do you check a solution found this way?
prompts.answer: Put both values into both original equations. It takes twenty seconds and catches any slip in the inverse or the product.

prompts.prompt: A question says to use a matrix method and you solve it correctly by elimination. What does that earn?
prompts.answer: Nothing. A named method is part of the question, and the examiners record correct elimination answers scoring zero.

prompts.prompt: What does a determinant of zero mean for a pair of simultaneous equations?
prompts.answer: The coefficient matrix has no inverse, so there is no unique solution: the two equations describe parallel lines.

findings.asked: Find an inverse; then solve simultaneous equations using the matrix method.
findings.wentWrong: The inverse was fine (a few wrote 26 instead of 1/-26). Many solved by elimination or substitution despite the instruction and received no marks; others struggled with the layout of the matrix method.
findings.rule: When told to use matrices, write X = A inverse B and multiply.

findings.asked: A matrix equation solved with an inverse.
findings.wentWrong: Well done; occasional multiplication in the wrong order; arithmetic slips.
findings.rule: Pre-multiply by the inverse: A inverse on the left of both sides.

findings.asked: Scalar multiple of a matrix; product of a 2x2 and a 2x3.
findings.wentWrong: A few squared the matrix instead of multiplying by the scalar; sign slips even with calculators.
findings.rule: A scalar multiplies every element; only matrix times matrix uses row-by-column.

insight.ruleToRemember: For AX = B, X = A inverse B with the inverse on the left; follow a stated method exactly - the algebra route scores nothing when the matrix method is required.
